headline: John Deere owners gain right to repair equipment under FTC settlement
summary: The Federal Trade Commission and several state attorneys general secured a landmark settlement, requiring Deere & Co. to provide diagnostic and repair tools to equipment owners and independent shops.
details: John Deere owners will soon be able to fix their own machines, following a right-to-repair settlement reached by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and attorneys general from Arizona, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin. This agreement mandates that Deere & Co. make its repair services, including software and diagnostic tools, available to equipment owners and independent shops.

For years, the Illinois-based manufacturer faced criticism for restricting access to necessary repair software, forcing customers to rely exclusively on authorized dealers. This new settlement aims to break that monopoly, allowing farmers and independent mechanics greater autonomy over their equipment maintenance.

The antitrust lawsuit, filed in January 2025, argued that Deere illegally restricted repairs of farm equipment like tractors. The order, awaiting approval from Judge Iain D. Johnston, also prevents Deere dealers from retaliating against those who choose independent repair options.

This marks the second right-to-repair resolution for Deere this year, following a $99 million class-action settlement with farmers in April. While the class-action provided compensation, the FTC's settlement directly addresses the systemic issue of repair access.

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes highlighted the impact, stating that farmers and mechanics were previously at the mercy of Deere's repair monopoly. Deere must also pay $1 million collectively to the five states for antitrust enforcement costs and will face strict compliance oversight for the next decade.

Deere maintained its commitment to independent repair in a statement, asserting that the agreement reinforces its efforts to innovate more flexible repair options. The company had previously denied that its service tool distribution was anticompetitive.

headline_marked: [[Brown University students' scores fell 50%]] on in-person final after AI cheating suspected on take-home midterm
headline: Brown University students' scores fell 50% on in-person final after AI cheating suspected on take-home midterm
summary: A Brown economics professor suspected widespread AI use after a take-home midterm averaged 96%. When he mandated an in-person final, the average score plummeted to 48%.
details: Brown University students in a difficult economics course saw their average score plummet from 96% to 48% on a final exam. This dramatic drop occurred after their professor, Roberto Serrano, switched from a take-home midterm to a supervised in-person final due to suspected AI cheating.

The course, ECON 1170, usually has few students, but 86 enrolled when take-home exams were announced. The midterm saw 40 students score a perfect 100, with an overall average of 96%, significantly higher than the historical 65-80% average for a harder exam.

Professor Serrano and his grad students noticed a "very convoluted style" in answers, even correct ones. Running exam questions through ChatGPT yielded similar results, solidifying his suspicions about AI assistance.

To test his theory, Serrano announced the final would be in-person, stating the midterm would be voided if final scores differed significantly. Following this, 18 students dropped the course and 9 didn't attend the final; 22 of these 27 had scored a perfect 100 on the midterm.

The resulting average score of 48% confirmed the professor's concerns about widespread academic dishonesty. This incident highlights the challenges universities face in maintaining academic integrity amidst the rise of generative AI tools.

Serrano, who went blind at 17, views challenges as optimization problems. His resolve underscores the seriousness with which some educators are approaching AI's impact on learning. Brown University is also addressing AI use, with a recent report on generative AI in teaching.
